riskClassification.title: Risk classification
riskClassification.intro: Classify the organization's AI systems using the EU AI Act four-tier risk framework. The classification form shows a rule screening of the system's registered facts (prohibited practices, Annex III areas, transparency duties) with a suggested level; you choose the level and, for high risk, the Annex III category. Every classification is kept in the history for audit purposes.
riskClassification.tiersIntro: The EU AI Act defines four risk levels. Each level carries different compliance obligations, from outright prohibition to minimal transparency requirements.

unacceptable.description: AI systems that pose an unacceptable risk to safety or fundamental rights. These are prohibited under Art. 5.
unacceptable.examples: Social scoring, real-time biometric identification in public spaces, manipulation techniques.

high.description: AI systems listed in Annex III or used as safety components. Subject to full compliance requirements (Art. 6-51).
high.examples: Biometric identification, critical infrastructure, employment decisions, law enforcement.

limited.description: AI systems with specific transparency obligations. Users must be informed they are interacting with AI (Art. 50).
limited.examples: Chatbots, deepfake generators, emotion recognition systems.

minimal.description: AI systems posing minimal risk. No mandatory compliance requirements, though voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged.
minimal.examples: Spam filters, AI-enabled video games, inventory management systems.

riskClassification.annexIntro: The classification form lists the Annex III high-risk categories. If the AI system falls into any of these areas, it is likely classified as High Risk.
riskClassification.historyIntro: Every classification change is versioned with a timestamp, the author, the previous and new risk levels, and a rationale. This provides a complete audit trail for regulators.

transparency.metaDescription: Track EU AI Act Art. 50 transparency obligations per AI system: AI interaction disclosure, synthetic-content marking, emotion recognition, and deepfake labeling.
transparency.title: Transparency (Art. 50)
transparency.intro: Article 50 of the EU AI Act imposes transparency duties that cut across risk tiers: even a minimal-risk chatbot owes a disclosure. AI SENTINEL tracks the four Art. 50 obligations per AI system, splits them by who actually owes them, and counts down the one deadline that has a transitional period.
transparency.applicabilityBody1: Art. 50 has applied since 2 August 2026 (Art. 113, second paragraph). Art. 111(4), inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the Digital Omnibus on AI, OJ L of 24 July 2026), gives providers of generative systems placed on the market before that date until 2 December 2026 to comply with the machine-readable marking duty in Art. 50(2).
transparency.applicabilityBody2: That grace period is the reason the registration of an AI system asks whether it was placed on the market before 2 August 2026. Answer it accurately: it is the only input that moves the marking deadline, and the dashboard's “marking overdue” counter is derived from it.
transparency.obligationsIntro: Two are owed by the provider and two by the deployer. A single organization often holds both roles, but recording them separately is what lets you answer a regulator asking which hat you were wearing.

obligations.title: AI interaction disclosure
obligations.description: Systems that interact directly with people must make clear they are AI, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person. Chatbots and voice agents are the typical case.

obligations.title: Machine-readable marking of synthetic content
obligations.description: Systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text must mark their output in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated. This is the obligation with a transitional deadline: see below.

obligations.title: Emotion recognition and biometric categorization
obligations.description: Deployers must inform the people exposed to an emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation system that it is in use. Note that several such uses are prohibited outright under Art. 5: the module flags that overlap rather than letting you record a disclosure for a practice you cannot lawfully run.

obligations.title: Deepfake and public-interest text labeling
obligations.description: Deployers publishing deepfakes must disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. The same applies to AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest.

statuses.name: Not applicable
statuses.description: This obligation does not apply to the system. The default for every obligation until you decide otherwise.

statuses.name: Required
statuses.description: The obligation applies and is not yet satisfied. Systems in this state drive the deadline counters on the executive dashboard.

statuses.name: Implemented
statuses.description: The obligation applies and the disclosure or marking is in place. Record how in the AI statement so the evidence survives staff turnover.

workingSteps.body: Every AI system in the registry has a Transparency (Art. 50) tab alongside Models, Data Sources, and Risk Classification.
The module screens the system's purpose and technique and suggests which of the four obligations look applicable. Treat these as prompts, not conclusions: you confirm each one.
Mark each as Not applicable, Required, or Implemented. Anything left Required appears in the dashboard's transparency counters.
Record the disclosure wording and the marking method you actually use. This is the artifact a market surveillance authority will ask for; a status field alone will not satisfy them.

transparency.scopeBody: This module records your Art. 50 position; it does not mark content for you. Machine-readable marking is implemented in the generating system itself. AI SENTINEL is where you document which systems owe the duty, whether it is satisfied, and how: so the answer exists before someone asks for it.

compliance.metaDescription: Framework mapping across nine frameworks (EU AI Act, GDPR, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, AIUC-1, California, Colorado, Texas and Washington) with evidence management and export.
compliance.title: Compliance
compliance.intro: Map the organization's AI systems against leading regulatory frameworks. Track compliance status at the requirement level, attach evidence, and export compliance packages for regulators and auditors.
compliance.frameworksIntro: AI SENTINEL ships with nine pre-loaded frameworks: three that apply by risk tier (the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001), five that apply by jurisdiction (the GDPR and the California, Colorado, Texas and Washington AI rules) and one you choose: AIUC-1, the certification standard for AI agents. Each framework is broken down into articles, clauses or functions with individual compliance tracking.

euAiAct.name: EU AI Act
euAiAct.description: Key-obligation mapping from Art. 4 (AI literacy) and Art. 5 (prohibited practices) through Art. 73 (serious incidents) and the Art. 113 applicability timeline, plus relevant annexes. The primary regulatory framework for AI systems in the European Union.

nist.name: NIST AI RMF
nist.description: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology AI Risk Management Framework. Four core functions with sub-categories.

iso.name: ISO 42001
iso.description: International standard for AI Management Systems. Covers organizational context, leadership, planning, support, and operations.
iso.items: {count} requirements: clauses 4 to 10 and Annex A controls

aiuc1.name: AIUC-1
aiuc1.description: AIUC-1, the certification standard for AI agents: six domains (data and privacy, security, safety, reliability, accountability, society), with mandatory technical testing at least every three months. It does not attach by risk tier: you choose it for your agents.
aiuc1.items: {count} requirements: six domains and the 51 requirements in force

gdpr.name: GDPR
gdpr.description: The AI-relevant articles of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, with Article 22 on solely automated decisions and Article 35 on impact assessments in full. Attaches by jurisdiction.

caAdmt.name: California CCPA ADMT
caAdmt.description: The California regulations on automated decision-making technology, risk assessments and cybersecurity audits. Attaches by jurisdiction.

colorado.name: Colorado SB 26-189
colorado.description: The statute that replaced the original Colorado AI Act: advance notice, post-decision disclosure, correction and review, and developer documentation. Attaches by jurisdiction.

texas.name: Texas TRAIGA
texas.description: House Bill 149: intent-based prohibitions, government and health care disclosure duties, and the NIST safe harbor. Attaches by jurisdiction.

washington.name: Washington
washington.description: Five instruments: consumer health data, content provenance, companion chatbots, prior authorization and public agencies. Attaches by jurisdiction.

compliance.statusesIntro: Each requirement can be independently assessed for every AI system. The status reflects the current compliance posture for that specific requirement.
compliance.matrixIntro: The compliance matrix provides a per-AI-system view of all requirements within a chosen framework. For each requirement, you can set the compliance status, add notes, and attach evidence documents.
compliance.crossIntro: Many requirements across the nine frameworks overlap. AI SENTINEL includes {count} pre-built cross-framework mappings, so that one piece of work can stand as evidence against several frameworks at once.
compliance.crossBody1: When you mark a requirement as <s>Compliant</s> or <s>Partially Compliant</s>, AI SENTINEL shows linked requirements from other frameworks and offers to propagate the status automatically.
compliance.crossBody2: For example, marking EU AI Act Art. 9 (Risk Management) as compliant can automatically update NIST GOVERN 1 (Risk Management Policies) and ISO 42001 Clause 6.1 (Actions to Address Risks): because they cover the same obligation.
compliance.snapshotBody1: When you classify an AI system's risk level (e.g., high risk under the EU AI Act), AI SENTINEL automatically creates compliance mapping records for every applicable requirement of the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001. The GDPR and the US state rules attach once the organization's jurisdictions and screening questions are answered. You arrive at the compliance matrix with the relevant controls pre-populated: no manual setup needed.
compliance.snapshotBody2: For a High Risk system, this means {count} requirements are initialized at once across the EU AI Act, the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001, each set to “Not Assessed” and ready for evaluation.

shadowAi.metaTitle: AI tools in use: AI SENTINEL Docs
shadowAi.metaDescription: Record the AI tools people in the organization use: a self-reporting portal, a triage workflow, and promotion to the organization's AI systems.
shadowAi.title: AI tools in use
shadowAi.intro: Shadow AI refers to AI tools adopted by employees without the knowledge or approval of the organization. Research suggests that around 60% of employees use unapproved AI tools at work: from ChatGPT and Copilot to image generators and AI-powered analytics. Organizations cannot govern AI systems they do not know about.
shadowAi.whatP1: Shadow AI is the AI equivalent of Shadow IT: the use of AI-powered tools, services, and applications by employees without explicit organizational authorization. Unlike formally procured vendors that go through risk assessment and contract review, shadow AI tools enter the organization through individual adoption: an engineer installs a code assistant, a lawyer uses ChatGPT for contract review, a marketing team signs up for an AI copywriting tool.
shadowAi.whatP2: Under the EU AI Act, organizations that deploy AI systems have specific obligations as deployers: regardless of whether the deployment was sanctioned or not. Shadow AI creates blind spots in compliance, data protection, and risk management programs.

whyItems.title: Compliance risk
whyItems.description: Unregistered AI systems may fall under high-risk categories without appropriate conformity assessments, human oversight, or risk documentation.

whyItems.title: Data protection
whyItems.description: Employees may input personal data, trade secrets, or client information into AI tools that train on user inputs or store data in non-compliant jurisdictions.

whyItems.title: Regulatory exposure
whyItems.description: Under the EU AI Act, deployers are responsible for AI systems used within their organization: even those adopted informally by staff.

whyItems.title: Governance gap
whyItems.description: You cannot classify risk, run assessments, or set oversight gates for AI systems you do not know exist. Shadow AI is the missing first step.

shadowAi.vsIntro: Shadow AI Discovery and Vendor Risk Management solve fundamentally different problems in opposite directions. They are complementary, not overlapping.

Known from day one: the org chose the vendor

howSteps.title: Triage and review

howSteps.title: Approve or prohibit
howSteps.description: Each tool is either APPROVED for continued use (with conditions) or PROHIBITED and flagged for removal. Prohibited tools trigger a clear organizational signal that the tool is not sanctioned.

howSteps.title: Promote to formal governance
howSteps.description: Approved shadow tools can be promoted into the AI Registry as a formal AI System (and optionally into a Vendor record) in a single step. This bridges informal discovery into the full governance program.

vendorCatalog.metaTitle: AI Vendor Catalog: AI SENTINEL Docs

vendorCatalog.title: AI vendor catalog
vendorCatalog.intro: Evaluating AI vendors from scratch is time-consuming and error-prone. The AI Vendor Catalog gives the governance team a head start with pre-populated profiles for more than 850 AI vendors: complete with risk indicators, compliance certifications, and deployment metadata.
vendorCatalog.whatTitle: What is the AI vendor catalog?
vendorCatalog.whatP1: The AI Vendor Catalog is a searchable, pre-populated directory of AI tool and service providers. Each vendor profile includes structured governance data: what the vendor does, where data is processed, what certifications they hold, whether they train on customer data, and their EU AI Act risk classification.
vendorCatalog.whatP2: The catalog is powered by <vw>VendorWatch</vw>, an independent AI vendor intelligence service that continuously audits and updates vendor profiles. Data syncs automatically, so the catalog stays current without manual research.

whyItems.title: Due diligence at scale
whyItems.description: Manually researching each AI vendor's data practices, certifications, and risk posture is impractical. The catalog provides a standardized baseline for every vendor evaluation.

whyItems.title: Faster procurement
whyItems.description: When a team requests a new AI tool, governance can check the catalog immediately: no weeks-long vendor questionnaire cycle needed for initial assessment.

whyItems.title: Regulatory compliance
whyItems.description: The EU AI Act requires deployers to understand the AI systems they use. Pre-classified vendor risk levels and compliance indicators help meet Art. 6 and Art. 26 obligations.

whyItems.title: Continuous updates
whyItems.description: Vendor risk profiles change as companies update their terms, certifications expire, or data practices evolve. Automated sync ensures the catalog reflects current reality.

conformity.metaDescription: EU AI Act Art. 43 conformity assessment template for high-risk AI systems. Structured evaluation of technical documentation, quality management, and post-market monitoring.
conformity.title: Conformity assessment
conformity.intro: High-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act must undergo a conformity assessment before being placed on the market. AI SENTINEL provides a structured template that walks the team through every requirement (from technical documentation to post-market monitoring) so nothing falls through the cracks.
conformity.whatP1: A conformity assessment is a formal evaluation process required by Art. 43 of the EU AI Act for high-risk AI systems. It verifies that the AI system meets all applicable requirements before deployment: covering data governance, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity.
conformity.whatP2: Depending on the use case, conformity assessments may be conducted internally by the provider or through a third-party notified body. In either case, the assessment must follow a structured methodology and produce documented evidence of compliance.

whoItems.title: AI Providers
whoItems.description: Organizations that develop or place high-risk AI systems on the EU market must complete a conformity assessment before deployment (Art. 16).

whoItems.title: AI Deployers
whoItems.description: Organizations deploying high-risk AI systems must verify that the provider has completed the conformity assessment and that the CE marking is in place (Art. 26).

whoItems.title: Annex III systems
whoItems.description: AI systems used in biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, or administration of justice (Art. 6(2)).

whoItems.title: Internal compliance teams
whoItems.description: Even when a notified body is involved, internal teams need a structured process to prepare documentation, gather evidence, and track remediation of gaps.

coversItems.description: Verification that a risk management system is established and maintained throughout the AI system lifecycle (Art. 9).
Assessment of training, validation, and testing data: including relevance, representativeness, and bias examination (Art. 10).
Review of technical documentation completeness: system description, design specifications, development process, and performance metrics (Art. 11, Annex IV).
Evaluation of automatic logging capabilities for traceability, including input/output records and system events (Art. 12).
Assessment of instructions for use, disclosure of AI nature, and interpretability measures for deployers and affected persons (Art. 13).
Verification that appropriate human oversight measures are designed into the system and documented (Art. 14).
Testing and validation of accuracy levels, resilience to errors and adversarial attacks, and cybersecurity measures (Art. 15).
Review of the provider's quality management system covering development processes, testing, and post-market obligations (Art. 17).
Verification that a post-market monitoring plan is in place to detect and address issues after deployment (Art. 72).

howSteps.title: Create a new assessment
howSteps.description: Select the Conformity Assessment template and link it to a registered AI system. The template pre-populates all required evaluation areas.

howSteps.title: Work through each section
howSteps.description: Each section presents structured questions aligned to the EU AI Act requirements. Record findings, attach evidence, and note any gaps.

howSteps.title: Submit for review
howSteps.description: Once complete, submit the assessment for review by the AI Officer or governance lead. The approval workflow tracks sign-off and any requested changes.

howSteps.title: Document and maintain
howSteps.description: The completed assessment becomes part of the organization's compliance record. Link it to the AI system's compliance mapping and revisit it when material changes occur.

biasFairness.metaTitle: Bias & Fairness Assessment: AI SENTINEL Docs
biasFairness.metaDescription: Structured bias and fairness evaluation for AI systems. Detect discrimination risks, assess protected attributes, and document mitigation measures.
biasFairness.title: Bias & fairness assessment
biasFairness.intro: AI systems can produce discriminatory outcomes: often unintentionally. The Bias & Fairness Assessment provides a structured methodology to evaluate the organization's AI systems for bias risks, document affected protected attributes, and track mitigation measures.
biasFairness.whatTitle: What is a bias & fairness assessment?
biasFairness.whatP1: A bias and fairness assessment is a systematic evaluation of an AI system's potential to produce outcomes that unfairly disadvantage individuals or groups based on protected characteristics: such as race, gender, age, disability, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status.
biasFairness.whatP2: Under the EU AI Act, providers of high-risk AI systems must examine training data for possible biases (Art. 10) and implement measures to prevent discriminatory outcomes. The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (Art. 21) explicitly prohibits discrimination, and AI systems that score, rank, or make decisions about people are particularly exposed to this risk.

whyItems.title: Legal obligation
whyItems.description: The EU AI Act requires bias examination of training data (Art. 10(2)(f)) and non-discrimination safeguards for high-risk systems. Failure to comply carries fines up to 3% of global turnover.

whyItems.title: Fundamental rights
whyItems.description: AI-driven discrimination can violate the right to non-discrimination (EU Charter Art. 21), equal treatment directives, and national equality legislation.

whyItems.title: Real-world impact
whyItems.description: Biased AI in hiring, credit scoring, healthcare triage, or law enforcement has documented consequences: rejected applicants, denied loans, missed diagnoses, and wrongful arrests.

whyItems.title: Reputational risk
whyItems.description: Public disclosure of biased AI outcomes causes lasting reputational damage. Proactive assessment demonstrates responsible AI governance to regulators, customers, and the public.

typesItems.description: Historical data reflects past discrimination. A hiring model trained on historical decisions inherits biases in who was previously hired or promoted.
The training dataset does not represent the population the system will serve. Underrepresented groups receive less accurate predictions.
The features or labels used as proxies are themselves biased. Using zip codes as a feature can encode racial segregation patterns.
A single model is applied to groups with different underlying distributions. Medical AI trained primarily on one demographic may underperform for others.
The system is used in a context different from the one it was designed for, or its outputs are interpreted in a biased manner by human operators.

coversItems.description: Identification of which protected characteristics (age, gender, race, disability, etc.) are relevant to the AI system's domain and affected population.
Evaluation of whether training and testing data adequately represents all relevant groups, including historically underrepresented populations.
Selection and application of appropriate fairness metrics: demographic parity, equalized odds, predictive parity, or individual fairness measures.
Analysis of whether ostensibly neutral features (location, language, education) serve as proxies for protected attributes.
Documentation of pre-processing, in-processing, or post-processing techniques used to reduce identified bias.
Ongoing monitoring strategy to detect bias drift after deployment, including thresholds and escalation procedures.

howSteps.title: Create a new assessment
howSteps.description: Select the Bias & Fairness template and link it to a registered AI system. The template structures the evaluation around the system's specific use case and affected population.

howSteps.title: Evaluate each dimension
howSteps.description: Work through the structured sections: identify relevant protected attributes, assess data representativeness, apply fairness metrics, and check for proxy variables.

howSteps.title: Document findings and mitigations
howSteps.description: Record identified bias risks with severity ratings. For each risk, document the mitigation approach: whether technical (algorithmic debiasing) or procedural (human review).

howSteps.title: Review and monitor
howSteps.description: Submit for approval, then establish ongoing monitoring. The assessment links to the AI system's record so bias findings inform risk classification and oversight decisions.

roles.metaDescription: Understand the five user roles in AI SENTINEL and what each role can do across all governance modules.
roles.title: Roles & permissions
roles.intro: AI SENTINEL uses five roles to control access to governance operations. Every action is enforced at the server level: the interface adapts to show only what your role allows.

owner.name: Owner
owner.summary: Full platform control. Team management, license activation, deleting the organization and all governance operations.

admin.name: Admin
admin.summary: Organization management and full governance access, without changing roles or deleting the organization.

aiOfficer.name: AI officer
aiOfficer.summary: Governance authority. Approves assessments, publishes policies, and makes oversight decisions.

member.name: Member
member.summary: Day-to-day governance work. Creates records, submits assessments, reports incidents.

viewer.name: Viewer
viewer.summary: Read-only access. Can view all dashboards, records, and reports but cannot make changes.

roles.hierarchyNote: Each role inherits all capabilities from the roles below it.

assign.creatorBody: The user who creates an organization is automatically assigned the <role>Owner</role> role.
assign.invitedBody: Users who are invited or who join via email domain matching receive the <role>Member</role> role by default. An Owner can change their role at any time.
assign.viewerBody: The Viewer role is assigned explicitly by an Owner or Admin. Viewers see a clean read-only interface: create and edit buttons are hidden, not just disabled.
assign.changesBody: Only the organization Owner can change member roles. All role changes are recorded in the audit trail.

roles.enforcementBody: All permissions are enforced at the API level, not just the interface. Even if a user crafts a direct API request, the server verifies their role and organization membership before processing any operation. This means security does not depend on what the browser shows or hides.

security.metaDescription: How AI SENTINEL protects the organization's data: records kept apart, access control, input validation, an audit trail, and where the data is stored.
security.title: Security & trust
security.intro: AI SENTINEL is built for organizations that manage sensitive AI governance data. Security is embedded in every layer of the platform: from how we isolate your data to how we control access and protect your information.

isolation.title: Data isolation
isolation.intro: Every organization's records are kept apart from every other organization's. Before the application shows or changes the organization's AI systems, assessments, policies, incidents or vendor data, it checks that you are a member of the organization.

items.title: Organization-Scoped Queries
items.description: Queries for the organization's governance records are filtered by the organization in each request handler.

items.title: Verified Membership
items.description: Before any operation on the organization's data, we verify that you are an active member of that organization. Membership is checked on every such request.

items.title: Cross-Tenant Protection
items.description: When a record points to another, the server checks that the other record is the organization's: a policy, data flow, oversight gate, incident, assessment, sensitive-data analysis or shadow AI report linked to an AI system; an AI system or data recipient linked to a vendor; and an assessment's template, which must be a shared template or one of yours.

items.title: Shared Reference Data Only
items.description: Only reference data (compliance frameworks, assessment templates, and the vendor and AI tool catalogs) is shared across organizations. Your governance data is never shared.

accessControl.title: Access control
accessControl.intro: AI SENTINEL enforces role-based access control (RBAC) on the server. Each change to governance records is checked against your role before it is carried out.
accessControl.readOnlyBody: Viewers have read-only access to governance records. Writes to those records are blocked at the server level, not just in the interface, so they cannot be made through API calls either.
accessControl.elevatedBody: Approving assessments, approving or publishing a policy, and passing, failing or deferring an oversight gate require the AI Officer, Admin or Owner role, whichever screen or API call makes the change. Billing actions are limited to Owners and Admins.

auth.title: Authentication
auth.intro: We support standard sign-in methods, with 12-hour sessions and rate-limited sign-in on the hosted service.

methods.title: Google OAuth
methods.description: Sign in with a Google account (OAuth 2.0)

methods.title: Magic Link
methods.description: Passwordless sign-in through a single-use link sent by email

methods.title: Cross-Platform SSO
methods.description: Single sign-on across the TODO.LAW apps (hosted service)

sessionItems: HTTP-only cookies prevent client-side access to session tokens
Secure cookie flag whenever the app is served over HTTPS
Sign-in requests carry a CSRF token
SameSite=Lax session cookies limit cross-site request forgery

validation.title: Input validation
validation.intro: All user inputs are validated on the server before reaching business logic. This protects against injection attacks and ensures data integrity.

items.title: Schema Validation
items.description: Every application (tRPC) input is validated against a strict schema, and integration endpoints check their fields in code. Invalid data is rejected before it reaches the database.

items.title: Parameterized Queries
items.description: All database queries use parameterized inputs, including the few written in SQL, which bind every value. This removes the risk of SQL injection.

items.title: Enum Enforcement
items.description: Status fields, risk levels, and categories use strict enum validation. Only predefined values are accepted.

audit.title: Audit trail
audit.intro: Changes to governance records and key decisions are logged to an audit trail. This supports compliance requirements and gives a record of governance activities.
audit.retentionBody: Audit records are kept when a member leaves the organization. When an organization is deleted, its records are deleted with it, including its audit history; one entry recording the deletion is kept.

transport.title: Transport & infrastructure
transport.intro: Your data is encrypted in transit with TLS, and at rest by the hosting and database providers' storage encryption.

items.title: HTTPS Everywhere
items.description: All connections are encrypted with TLS. HSTS headers ensure browsers always use secure connections.

items.title: Clickjacking Protection
items.description: Security headers prevent the application from being embedded in frames on other sites.

items.title: Content Security
items.description: MIME-type sniffing prevention and strict referrer policies protect against content-based attacks.

items.title: Minimal Permissions
items.description: Browser APIs (camera, microphone, geolocation) are explicitly disabled: the application never requests unnecessary access.

items.title: Where the data is stored
items.description: On the TODO.LAW cloud, if an admin turns AI features on, the text they use goes to the AI provider set up on the service. On a managed instance or on your own hardware, the data stays there, unless you connect an external AI provider.

api.title: API security
api.intro: Every endpoint that reads or changes organization data requires authentication. External integrations use signature verification and key-based authentication.
api.endpointBody: Every governance endpoint used by the application requires an authenticated session with verified organization membership. Unauthenticated requests are rejected.
api.webhookBody: Inbound integration requests are authenticated with an API key, and webhooks use cryptographic signature verification. Unverified requests are discarded before processing.

backups.title: Backups and recovery
backups.cloud: On our cloud, each product's database is kept in Frankfurt (EU) and encrypted at rest with AES-256. We keep a continuous history of changes for 7 days, so we can recover the database as it was at any moment in that week, and a daily copy of the whole database kept for 30 days, in the same region. Only our named staff can reach these copies, with two-factor authentication.
backups.recovery: If something goes wrong, we aim to restore the service within one business day. If you ask, we recover your organization's records as they were at an earlier moment within those periods, without affecting other customers, at no charge and within two business days. We test a recovery every quarter and record the date.
backups.deletion: Deleted data leaves every copy within 30 days. You can export everything at any time.
backups.selfHosted: On your own hardware, AI Sentinel includes a script that makes encrypted database backups; you set the schedule and keep the copies.

standards.title: Security standards

crossBorder.metaTitle: Cross-border AI governance: one assessment, six regimes | AI SENTINEL
crossBorder.metaDescription: Answer the EU AI Act, the GDPR, California ADMT, Colorado, Texas and Washington from a single impact assessment, and generate the notice and appeal protocol that follow.
crossBorder.title: Cross-border regimes
crossBorder.intro: Most organizations deploying AI answer to several regulators at once, and each asks a version of the same question in different words. AI SENTINEL resolves which regimes reach each system, asks one question set drafted to the strictest of them, and generates the documents each regime expects.
crossBorder.architectureBody1: The assessment has a common core that is always asked. Each core question is drafted to the strictest formulation among the regimes, so answering it once satisfies every regime that asks a weaker version of the same thing.
crossBorder.architectureBody2: On top of that core sit jurisdictional overlays. An overlay question appears only when that regime's rules have put the system in scope, so a European deployer is never asked about Washington health carriers, and a Texas-only business never sees a California section number.
crossBorder.architectureBody3: Every question declares which requirement codes its answer evidences. That is what lets one answer stand as evidence in several compliance registers at the same time, and it is what the generated documents cite.

regimes.name: EU AI Act
regimes.detail: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Risk classification, Annex III screening, the Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment, Article 50 transparency, Annex IV technical documentation and the obligation calendar.

regimes.name: GDPR
regimes.detail: The AI-relevant articles, with Article 22 on solely automated decisions and Article 35 on impact assessments in full, including the CJEU reading that an automatically generated score can itself be the decision.

regimes.name: California CCPA ADMT
regimes.detail: The OAL-approved regulations: the three-prong human-involvement test, significant-decision domains, pre-use notice, opt-out, access, and the risk-assessment regime that has been live since January 2026.

regimes.name: Colorado SB 26-189
regimes.detail: The replacement statute that repealed the original Colorado AI Act. Advance notice, post-decision disclosure, correction and review, and developer documentation. Effective 1 January 2027, subject to pending federal litigation.

regimes.name: Texas TRAIGA
regimes.detail: House Bill 149, in force since January 2026. Intent-based prohibitions, government and health care disclosure duties, the NIST safe harbor and the regulatory sandbox.

regimes.name: Washington
regimes.detail: No single act, so five instruments: the My Health My Data Act for algorithmic health inference, HB 1170 provenance (2026 c 167, from 1 February 2027), HB 2225 companion chatbots (2026 c 168, from 1 January 2027), the prior-authorisation limits on AI-only denials in RCW 48.43.830 (in force since 11 June 2026), and RCW 43.105 for public agencies.

crossBorder.scopeBody: Each regime has its own deterministic rules module. It reads the jurisdictions the organization has declared plus a handful of screening answers, and returns one of three states.

scopeStates.name: Applies
scopeStates.description: The regime reaches this system, and its overlay questions and requirements attach.

scopeStates.name: Does not apply
scopeStates.description: Someone answered the questions that rule it out. This is an assertion, so it is only ever made from answers a person actually gave.

scopeStates.name: Undetermined
scopeStates.description: Nobody has answered yet. Nothing attaches, and the state is shown as an open question rather than being read as a no. An unanswered question is a visible gap, never a silent one.

crossBorder.reuseBody: Where two regimes ask the same legal question, the product reuses the answer rather than asking twice. A California ADMT determination that finds the technology is the sole factor in a significant decision also answers the GDPR Article 22 question, and a positive determination with a named decision domain answers the Colorado covered-technology test. The assessment records which answer it inferred from, so the reasoning stays auditable.
crossBorder.artifactsBody: From one answered assessment the product assembles four documents. Assembly is deterministic: no model is called, so a document that cites statute is reproducible and every sentence traces to an answer. They download as Markdown so they can go straight into the organization's own systems of record.

artifacts.name: Unified impact assessment
artifacts.description: One record answering the EU AI Act fundamental rights impact assessment, the GDPR data protection impact assessment, the California risk assessment and the state regimes.

artifacts.name: Multi-jurisdictional AI notice
artifacts.description: A universal core drafted to the strictest regime, plus one addendum for each jurisdiction that adds obligations of its own. The addenda never mix.

artifacts.name: Human review and appeal protocol
artifacts.description: One review workflow satisfying GDPR Article 22(3), the California human-appeal exception, the Colorado review right and the EU AI Act right to an explanation, with a table of what each jurisdiction words differently.

artifacts.name: Agentic addendum
artifacts.description: The stress test as a document: where each of the three breaks when the system hands off to an autonomous agent, and the provisions that layer demands.

crossBorder.gapsBody: An unanswered question does not silently drop the paragraph it would have filled. It becomes a visible gap carrying the obligation it would have evidenced, and every gap is collected into an open-items summary at the top of the document. A generated document that quietly omits an unanswered obligation is worse than no document, because it reads as complete.
crossBorder.agenticBody1: Every regime in this product was written for a system that produces an output which a person then uses. An autonomous agent that acts on that output breaks that assumption in a different place in each regime.
crossBorder.agenticBody2: The stress test runs eleven findings over the system, each naming the document it breaks, the assumption the regime made, what the handoff does to it, and the provision the agentic layer demands. Findings are gated on the regimes that actually apply, so a Texas deployer is not shown a GDPR failure.

agenticExamples.name: The Article 22 boundary moves to the agent
agenticExamples.description: Your analysis said the decision is not solely automated because a person reviews the output. If an agent then acts on it and nobody reviews the action, the decision the person experiences is solely automated after all.

agenticExamples.name: The human-involvement prongs fail at the handoff
agenticExamples.description: The California test requires a reviewer with authority to change the decision. An agent that executes before review completes removes that authority in practice, and the test is conjunctive.

agenticExamples.name: The protocol reviews what cannot be reversed
agenticExamples.description: With an agent in the chain the action is often complete before anyone appeals. Review without reversal is not the human intervention the GDPR requires.

threatModel.metaDescription: Start from the system you are building: what could go wrong, what stops it, and whether that was tested.
threatModel.title: Threat modeling
threatModel.intro: Telling a five-person team to implement a governance framework is not helpful. Asking what could go wrong with the thing they are actually building is. This module makes that question systematic, and does most of the writing for you.
threatModel.intro2: It takes about thirty minutes with the people who built the system, and it produces a record a customer's security review, an auditor or a regulator can read.

loop.body: What the system can see, retrieve, remember, call and do. This is the only step that needs thinking.
What could go wrong: by accident, by attack, or in ordinary use. The product proposes the list.
By impact, likelihood and blast radius. Computed, so two people rating the same facts get the same answer.
Prevent, constrain, detect, respond, assure. Each scenario arrives with controls already drafted.
Try to break the control and record what happened. Repeat when the system changes.

threatModel.mapIntro: Tick what is true today, not what is planned. Everything else follows from these answers.

questions.name: What can it see?
questions.body: User input, customer records, employee records, health or other sensitive data, payment data, credentials.

questions.name: What can it retrieve?
questions.body: Internal documents, web pages, email, source code. Anything retrieved is untrusted data.

questions.name: What does it remember?
questions.body: The conversation, or a profile that persists. Memory that persists can be poisoned once and used many times.

questions.name: What can it call?
questions.body: Tools, a database, code or shell commands, third-party services. Each one is a way for a manipulated model to act.

questions.name: What can it do?
questions.body: Send messages outside, move money, change records, deploy code, influence a decision about a person, hand off to another agent.

threatModel.backIntro: Concrete scenarios, each with controls at the right layers and a test written so you can run it this afternoon. Five capabilities typically produce eight scenarios and around twenty controls.

examples.name: It answers with a document the person was not allowed to see
examples.body: Authorization at retrieval, with the asker's own permissions. Test: ask the same question as three people with different permissions.

examples.name: A retrieved document tells it what to do, and it obeys
examples.body: Treat retrieved bytes as data, keep the tool allowlist narrow after external content. Test: plant an instruction and check it is not followed.

examples.name: It pays out far more than anyone intended
examples.body: A cap on what happens without a person, and approval above it. Test: try to beat the cap three ways, including through a document.

examples.name: It works exactly as designed and still treats a group worse
examples.body: Named decision factors, proxy checks, outcome monitoring after deployment. Test: run the same cases with one characteristic varied.

threatModel.layersIntro: An empty layer is the finding. A system with four preventive controls and nothing that detects will learn of its first incident from a customer.

layers.name: Prevent
layers.body: Access control, input validation, least privilege, sandboxing.

layers.name: Constrain
layers.body: Transaction limits, scoped credentials, restricted APIs, bounded autonomy.

layers.name: Respond
layers.body: A stop switch, rollback, revoked credentials, terminated sessions.

layers.name: Assure
layers.body: Red teaming, adversarial tests, evaluations, regression tests.

threatModel.testedIntro: "We have a guardrail" is not evidence. A control has one of four states, and only one of them counts.

states.name: Untested
states.body: Nobody has tried to break it. It is a claim.

states.name: Not holding
states.body: The last test failed, or passed only in part. A half-working control is not a control.

states.name: Test out of date
states.body: It passed, more than six months ago. Systems change; the test has to be repeated.

states.name: Tested
states.body: A passing test within the last six months. This is the only state that evidences anything.

threatModel.registerTitle: What this proves in the compliance register
threatModel.registerBody1: A control with a current passing test can be written into the compliance register as evidence, against the obligations it meets: accuracy and robustness, human oversight, record-keeping, security of processing, and the matching NIST and ISO entries.
threatModel.registerBody2: An untested control writes nothing, on purpose. The screen shows which scenarios evidence nothing yet, which is the work still to do. Applying twice writes nothing the second time.

screening.title: California CCPA screening
screening.description: Five answers that decide which California duties reach the organization. Anything left unanswered stays visibly unanswered: we never read silence as “no”.
screening.auditIntro: The next three decide the Article 9 cybersecurity audit under § 7120(b). Revenue band alone never puts you in scope: it only selects the phase-in tier once you already are.

coveredBusiness.label: Is the organization a “business” under the CCPA?
coveredBusiness.help: Met by any one of: annual gross revenue above the CPI-adjusted threshold ($26,625,000 for 2025–2026); buying, selling or sharing the personal information of 100,000+ consumers or households; or deriving 50% or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing personal information. There is no small-business exemption, the thresholds are the carve-out.

sellShareRevenue50Plus.label: Does 50% or more of annual revenue come from selling or sharing personal information?
sellShareRevenue50Plus.help: On its own this puts the organization into the Article 9 cybersecurity-audit regime.

revenueOverCcpaThreshold.label: Is annual gross revenue above the CPI-adjusted CCPA threshold?
revenueOverCcpaThreshold.help: $26,625,000 for 2025–2026. The next CPI adjustment is due 1 January 2027 and has not been published. Asked separately from the revenue band because the under-$50M band spans both sides of this figure.

largeProcessingVolume.label: Did the organization process the personal information of 250,000+ consumers or households, or the sensitive personal information of 50,000+ consumers, last calendar year?
largeProcessingVolume.help: Combined with the previous answer, this is the second route into the Article 9 audit duty.

revenueBand.label: Which revenue band applies, for the audit phase-in?
revenueBand.help: Selects the § 7121(a) deadline once you are in scope: over $100M reports by 1 April 2028, $50M–$100M by 1 April 2029, under $50M by 1 April 2030. Each tier measures a different revenue year.

isPublicAgency.label: Is the organization a public agency or governmental entity?
isPublicAgency.help: Texas TRAIGA adds disclosure and social-scoring duties for government; Washington RCW 43.105 governs agency use of automated decision systems.

isHealthCarrier.label: Is the organization a health carrier making prior-authorisation decisions?
isHealthCarrier.help: Washington RCW 48.43.830 bars an AI tool from denying, delaying or modifying coverage on its own.

isHealthcareProvider.label: Is the organization a health care service provider?
isHealthcareProvider.help: Texas TRAIGA requires telling the patient when AI is used in their care.

isCoveredGenAiProvider.label: Does the organization provide a generative AI system with more than one million monthly users, publicly available in Washington?
isCoveredGenAiProvider.help: That is the covered-provider test in Washington HB 1170, which requires provenance data in generated media.

processesConsumerHealthData.label: Does the organization process consumer health data of Washington consumers?
processesConsumerHealthData.help: The My Health My Data Act includes health inferred by algorithms from non-health information.

solelyAutomatedLegalEffect.label: Is this a decision based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects?
solelyAutomatedLegalEffect.help: GDPR Art. 22. A reviewer who only confirms the output does not take the decision outside it.

processesSpecialCategoryData.label: Does the system process or infer special-category data?
processesSpecialCategoryData.help: Health, biometric, genetic, racial or ethnic origin, political, religious, trade-union, sex life or sexual orientation. Inferences count.

materiallyInfluencesConsequentialDecisio.label: Does the system materially influence a consequential decision about a consumer?
materiallyInfluencesConsequentialDecisio.help: Colorado SB 26-189: education, employment, housing, financial or lending services, insurance, health care, legal services or essential government services.

isCompanionChatbot.label: Is this an AI companion chatbot?
isCompanionChatbot.help: Washington HB 2225: adaptive, human-like responses capable of sustaining a relationship across sessions.

usedInPriorAuthorization.label: Is the system used in prior-authorisation determinations?
usedInPriorAuthorization.help: Washington RCW 48.43.830. The tool may approve; it may not deny.

interactsWithConsumers.label: Do consumers interact with this system directly?

handsOffToAutonomousAgent.label: Does this system hand its output to an autonomous agent that can act without a person?
handsOffToAutonomousAgent.help: This is what the agentic stress test examines. No statute keys off it yet, which is precisely the gap the agentic addendum documents.

agent.description: How much this system does on its own, what it may reach, who is accountable and who can stop it. Every regime in this product assumes a system that produces an output a person then uses; an agent that acts on that output changes what each one asks of you.
agent.autonomyLabel: How much does it do on its own?

agent.fieldActionScopeHelp: A bounded list of action categories, not a general objective. An unconstrained objective is the fact a regulator will read as intent.
agent.fieldDownstream: Which agents or systems receive its output?
agent.fieldDownstreamHelp: Anything that acts further on what this system produces.
agent.fieldTools: Tools and services it may call
agent.fieldToolsHelp: One per line. An agent reaches further than the system's own contract does, so this is the list that has to sit inside the organization's processing agreement.

agent.fieldReversalHelp: Review without reversal is not the human intervention the GDPR requires.

agent.fieldTraceabilityHelp: The decision, the model version and the data behind it.

applicability.stepTitle: Before starting: what applies to the organization
applicability.stepLead: A few plain questions decide which laws and frameworks apply to the organization, and switch them on. Answer what you can. "Not sure yet" is a fair answer.
applicability.skip: I'm not sure yet, skip this for now

buildsForOthers.label: Does the organization build AI systems that others use (as a provider)?
buildsForOthers.hint: For example, a product with AI features that the organization sells or gives to customers.

usesAi.label: Does the organization use AI systems in its own work (as a deployer)?
usesAi.hint: For example, chat assistants, writing tools, or AI inside software the organization buys.

generalPurposeModel.label: Does the organization sell or offer a general-purpose AI model?
generalPurposeModel.hint: A model that others build on, such as a large language model offered through an API.

meetsPeople.label: Does any of the organization's AI talk to people or produce content they see?
meetsPeople.hint: Chatbots, voice assistants, and generated text, images, audio or video.

decidesAboutPeople.label: Does any of the organization's AI help decide about people?
decidesAboutPeople.hint: In employment, credit, housing, education, health, insurance or essential services.

usesAgents.label: Does the organization use AI agents that act on their own?
usesAgents.hint: Systems that take actions, such as sending messages or changing records, without a person approving each one.

wantsCertification.label: Does the organization want a management system that can be certified?
wantsCertification.hint: ISO/IEC 42001 is the certifiable standard for an AI management system.

quickstart.label: Quick start
quickstart.why: It sets the jurisdictions, applies an industry template and imports the vendors from the catalog, so the rest of the program starts filled in.
quickstart.do: Answer a few questions, and a first version of the program is filled in.
quickstart.doneWhen: the quick start has been run to the end once, or a system, a vendor and a policy already exist.

obligations.label: Where the organization operates and the rules that apply
obligations.why: The rules that apply depend on where the organization operates. Declare the places and answer the short questions on this step's page, so the rules and their dates are the ones that apply.
obligations.do: Declare where the organization operates and answer the questions on this page. Then it lists the rules that apply and their dates.
obligations.doneWhen: the places are declared and every screening shown for them is answered.

policies.label: AI policy
policies.why: An approved acceptable-use policy tells everyone which AI tools they may use, and how.
policies.do: Write and approve the policy that says which AI tools people may use, and how.
policies.doneWhen: an acceptable-use policy is approved or published.

prohibited.label: Banned uses check
prohibited.why: A check of every use against the practices the EU AI Act bans.
prohibited.do: Check that no use of AI is one the law bans.

literacy.label: AI training
literacy.why: A record of the AI training given to the people who use or oversee AI.
literacy.do: Record the AI training given to the people who use or oversee AI.

systems.label: The organization's AI systems
systems.why: Every system needs a record and an owner before its risk can be set.
systems.do: Register each AI system the organization uses and name who owns it.
systems.doneWhen: at least one AI system is registered and every system has a business owner.

shadowAi.label: AI tools in use
shadowAi.why: Record the AI tools people already use, then decide on each one.
shadowAi.do: List the AI tools people use and decide on each one still to review.
shadowAi.doneWhen: at least one AI tool in use is recorded and none is still to review.

vendors.label: Vendors
vendors.why: Most AI reaches the organization through vendors. Add them from the vendor catalog.
vendors.do: Add the companies whose AI the organization uses. The vendor catalog makes it quick.
vendors.doneWhen: at least one vendor is recorded.

classification.label: Risk level
classification.why: The risk level of each system decides which rules apply to it.
classification.do: Give each AI system its risk level. The level decides which rules apply.
classification.doneWhen: every system has a risk level confirmed by a person.

assessments.label: Impact assessments
assessments.why: High-risk systems need an approved impact assessment.
assessments.do: Assess each high-risk system and have the assessment approved.
assessments.doneWhen: at least one assessment is approved and every high-risk system has an approved one.

threatModel.label: Threat model
threatModel.why: Write down what could go wrong with the systems the organization builds, and how each risk is stopped and tested.
threatModel.do: Write down what could go wrong with the AI the organization builds, and how each risk is stopped and tested.
threatModel.doneWhen: at least one threat model is past draft.

vendorDueDiligence.label: Vendor checks
vendorDueDiligence.why: Each vendor needs a completed review.
vendorDueDiligence.do: Check each vendor: open it and answer its review (agreement, data location, certifications). About twenty minutes each.
vendorDueDiligence.doneWhen: every vendor has a completed due-diligence review.

agentTesting.label: Test the organization's AI agents (AIUC-1)
agentTesting.why: Before the AIUC-1 audit, each AI agent needs every requirement that applies to it tested and passed, or a partial result accepted.
agentTesting.do: Test each AI agent against AIUC-1: record what you did and the result, until every requirement that applies has passed.
agentTesting.doneWhen: every AI agent is ready for the AIUC-1 audit.

oversight.label: Human oversight
oversight.why: High-risk systems need a person who can review, approve or stop them.
oversight.do: Name a person who can review, approve or stop each high-risk system.
oversight.doneWhen: every high-risk system has a confirmed oversight gate (with no high-risk system, at least one confirmed gate exists).

transparency.label: Telling people it is AI
transparency.why: Record for each system whether people must be told they are dealing with AI (Art. 50).
transparency.do: For each system, record whether people must be told they are dealing with AI. Open a system to do it.
transparency.doneWhen: every system has a transparency profile confirmed by a person.

evidence.label: Evidence
evidence.why: Give each requirement a status and attach the proof that supports it.
evidence.do: Choose a system, give each requirement a status and attach the proof.
evidence.doneWhen: every mapped requirement has a status and at least one piece of evidence is attached.

sensitiveData.label: Sensitive data
sensitiveData.why: Classify the sensitive data the organization's systems use, starting with personal data.
sensitiveData.do: Check the sensitive data the organization's systems use, starting with personal data.
sensitiveData.doneWhen: at least one sensitive-data assessment exists and every system that processes personal data has one.

incidents.label: Incidents
incidents.why: Approve an incident plan so everyone knows what to do and the legal deadlines are met.
incidents.do: Approve an incident plan so everyone knows what to do and the legal deadlines are met.
incidents.doneWhen: an incident-response policy is approved or published.

proceedings.label: Cases and inquiries
proceedings.why: Track an inquiry or a case from an authority or a court, if there is one.
proceedings.do: Track an inquiry or a case from an authority or a court, if there is one.
proceedings.doneWhen: every proceeding is closed. Needed only when there is one.

review.label: Check what was drafted
review.why: What the product drafted for you counts only once a person confirms it.
review.do: Confirm or correct what the product drafted for you. It counts once a person confirms it.
review.doneWhen: nothing drafted is waiting for a person to confirm it.

board.label: Board report
board.why: Report the state of the program to the board, with figures that can be reproduced.
board.do: Tell the board where the program stands, with figures that can be reproduced.
board.doneWhen: at least one board report exists.

audit.why: Every change is recorded here on its own.
audit.do: See every change made in the program. It is recorded on its own.
audit.doneWhen: the product keeps it on its own, from the first recorded change.

agentTesting.readyRule: An agent is ready for the audit when every requirement that applies to it has a pass from the last three months, or a partial result a person has accepted.
agentTesting.readyExplained: Every requirement that applies has a current pass or an accepted partial result. The audit itself is done by an accredited third party.

domainAbout.B: Defending the agent against manipulation: adversarial input, prompt injection, scraping and actions it was not allowed to take.

domainAbout.D: Preventing made-up answers and unsafe tool calls, with testing and control of the tools the agent may call.
domainAbout.E: Who answers when something goes wrong, how changes are approved, what is logged, and how vendors are checked.
domainAbout.F: Preventing the agent from being misused for cyber attacks, manipulation or catastrophic harm.

defaultDescription.AI_USAGE: Sets out which AI tools staff may use, for which purposes and with which data, and the human review required before AI output is relied on.
defaultDescription.AI_GOVERNANCE: Sets out who is responsible for AI in the organization, how AI systems are recorded, classified by risk and approved, and how their use is overseen and reviewed.
defaultDescription.AI_ETHICS: Sets out the principles the organization applies when it develops, buys or uses AI, and how concerns are raised and decided.
defaultDescription.AI_RISK_MANAGEMENT: Sets out how the organization identifies, assesses, reduces and monitors the risks of its AI systems, and who accepts the risks that remain.
defaultDescription.AI_DATA_GOVERNANCE: Sets out the rules for the data used to train, test, prompt and operate AI systems, including lawful basis, data quality, retention and transfers.
defaultDescription.AI_PROCUREMENT: Sets out the checks and contract terms required before the organization buys, licenses or trials an AI product or service, and when they are repeated.
defaultDescription.AI_INCIDENT_RESPONSE: Sets out how AI incidents are reported, assessed and contained, how they are notified to authorities or affected people where the law requires, and how lessons are recorded.
defaultDescription.AI_TRANSPARENCY: Sets out when and how the organization tells people that AI is used, how AI-generated content is marked, and how decisions involving AI are explained.
defaultDescription.CUSTOM: Sets out the purpose, scope and rules of this policy, who it applies to and who is responsible for it.
